summary: Defines S/MIME version 3.1, a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures give authentication, integrity and proof of origin, encryption gives confidentiality, and compression can also be used. It was replaced by RFC 5751.

plainLanguage.summary: S/MIME 3.1 adds three services to a mail message: a signature that shows who sent it and that it was not changed, encryption that keeps the text private, and compression that makes it smaller. It defines the message formats, the algorithms that must be supported, and how a sender picks the encryption to use.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with smime
subtitle: The message formats, algorithms and rules used to sign and encrypt mail with S/MIME version 3.1.

tldr.problem: Mail systems need one agreed way to prove who sent a message, prove it was not altered, and keep its contents private, and the rules have to be the same on both ends of the wire.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME wraps a MIME body in a Cryptographic Message Syntax object of type SignedData, EnvelopedData or CompressedData, and carries that object in the application/pkcs7-mime type, or as a detached signature in a multipart/signed message. The RFC also fixes the minimum set of algorithms that every implementation must handle.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3851 was a Proposed Standard and it obsoleted RFC 2633. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 5751.

today: RFC 3851 was a Proposed Standard published in July 2004 and it obsoleted RFC 2633. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 5751.

sections.title: What S/MIME 3.1 Provides
sections.content:
S/MIME provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Based on the MIME standard, it offers authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin using digital signatures, and data confidentiality using encryption, with message compression as a supplementary service.

It can be used by traditional mail user agents to add these services to mail they send and to interpret them in mail they receive, but it is not restricted to mail. It can be used with any transport mechanism that transports MIME data, such as HTTP, and it can be used in automated message transfer agents that need no human intervention, for example to sign software-generated documents or to encrypt FAX messages sent over the Internet.

The specification defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is derived from PKCS #7. It also defines the application/pkcs7-mime type used to carry those body parts, and it discusses how to use the multipart/signed type, with the application/pkcs7-signature type, to transport signed messages.

Requirements and recommendations are separated for receiving agents and sending agents, in the general spirit of being liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send. An S/MIME agent MUST follow this document and the Cryptographic Message Syntax document when it creates messages. Agents for version 3.1 SHOULD try to have the greatest interoperability possible with agents for earlier versions: version 2 is described in RFC 2311 to RFC 2315 and version 3 in RFC 2630 to RFC 2634.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME 3.1 adds a signature, encryption and compression to a mail message. It works with any transport that carries MIME data, and it is designed so that old and new mail clients can still read each other's messages.

sections.title: Required Algorithms and Content Types
sections.content:
CMS allows a wide variety of options in content and algorithm support, so this section sets a base level of interoperability that every S/MIME implementation must meet.

For the digest algorithm, sending and receiving agents MUST support SHA-1, and receiving agents SHOULD support MD5, so that MD5-digested S/MIME version 2 SignedData objects can still be read. For the signature algorithm, receiving agents MUST support id-dsa-with-sha1, with the algorithm parameters absent rather than encoded as NULL, and MUST support rsaEncryption. Sending agents MUST support either id-dsa-with-sha1 or rsaEncryption, and if they use rsaEncryption they MUST support the digest algorithms of the previous section as specified. For the key encryption algorithm, sending and receiving agents MUST support rsaEncryption and SHOULD support Diffie-Hellman in ephemeral-static mode.

Four CMS content types are used for S/MIME. Data identifies the inner MIME message content, and a sending agent MUST use the id-data content type identifier for it. SignedData applies a digital signature to a message, providing authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin, and is also used in the degenerate case where there is no signature information, to convey certificates. EnvelopedData applies data confidentiality, and the sender needs a public key for each intended recipient. CompressedData applies compression to reduce the message size and provides none of the security services.

Section 2.5 adds the signed attributes that travel with a signature. Receiving agents MUST be able to handle zero or one instance of each of signingTime, sMIMECapabilities, sMIMEEncryptionKeyPreference, id-messageDigest and id-contentType, and sending agents SHOULD generate one instance of each in every S/MIME message, together with the signingCertificate attribute. The SMIMECapabilities attribute is the list of algorithms a client can handle, in order of preference, and it is what lets a sender pick an encryption method the recipient will be able to read.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets a minimum set of algorithms so that two implementations can talk to each other: SHA-1 for the digest, DSA with SHA-1 or RSA for signatures, RSA for key encryption, and tripleDES for the content itself. A signed message also carries a list of the algorithms the sender can handle.

sections.title: How an S/MIME Message Is Built
sections.content:
An S/MIME message is a combination of MIME bodies and CMS content types. The data to be secured is always a canonical MIME entity. The MIME entity and other data, such as certificates and algorithm identifiers, are given to CMS processing, which produces a CMS object, and the CMS object is then wrapped in MIME.

The application/pkcs7-mime type carries CMS content types including EnvelopedData, SignedData and CompressedData. Because these are binary, base-64 transfer encoding is appropriate in most cases, in particular with SMTP transport, though the transfer encoding depends on the transport and is not a characteristic of the media type. The Content-Type header field of all application/pkcs7-mime objects SHOULD include the optional smime-type parameter, so that a receiving agent can tell what is inside without decoding the ASN.1. The values are enveloped-data for EnvelopedData, signed-data for SignedData, certs-only for a SignedData object with no content, and compressed-data for CompressedData. The file extensions are .p7m for SignedData and EnvelopedData, .p7c for a certificate management message, .p7z for CompressedData and .p7s for application/pkcs7-signature.

A certificate management message is used to transport certificates and certificate revocation lists, for example in response to a registration request. The certificates are given to the CMS process, which creates a SignedData object whose encapContentInfo eContent field is absent and whose signerInfos field is empty, and the resulting object is wrapped in an application/pkcs7-mime entity with the smime-type parameter certs-only and the extension .p7c.

Because S/MIME has to work outside MIME environments, identifying a message takes some care. A message counts as an S/MIME message if it matches any of these: the MIME type is application/pkcs7-mime with any parameters and any file suffix; the MIME type is multipart/signed with the parameter protocol set to application/pkcs7-signature and any file suffix; or the MIME type is application/octet-stream with any parameters and a file suffix of p7m, p7s, p7c or p7z.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed or encrypted content is put in a standard MIME shape, wrapped in a CMS object, and carried in a body part whose type says what it is. A certificate-only message carries certificates and revocation lists with no signature in it.

sections.title: Signed, Enveloped and Compressed Messages
sections.content:
For an enveloped-only message, the MIME entity is prepared, processed into a CMS object of type EnvelopedData, wrapped in a CMS ContentInfo object and inserted into an application/pkcs7-mime entity, with the smime-type enveloped-data and the extension .p7m. In addition to encrypting a copy of the content-encryption key for each recipient, a copy SHOULD be encrypted for the originator and included. The RFC warns that an enveloped message that is not signed does not provide data integrity, because the ciphertext can be replaced in a way that still processes correctly while changing the meaning.

For a signed-only message there are two formats: application/pkcs7-mime with SignedData, and multipart/signed. The multipart/signed form is preferred for sending, and receiving agents MUST be able to handle both. It is a clear-signing format, so recipients without S/MIME or CMS facilities can still read the message, and any other MIME structure in the message survives. The multipart/signed type has two parts: the first holds the MIME entity that is signed, and the second holds the detached signature CMS SignedData object, whose encapContentInfo eContent field is absent. That second part is an application/pkcs7-signature entity with the extension .p7s. The multipart/signed Content-Type has two required parameters, protocol and micalg. The protocol parameter MUST be application/pkcs7-signature, quoted because MIME requires the slash to be quoted. The micalg parameter names the message digest algorithm or algorithms, separated by commas, and lets the signature be verified in one pass; the values are md5, sha1, sha256, sha384 and sha512, with a note that the SHA-2 algorithms are included for completeness and are not currently recommended in S/MIME.

A compressed-only message produces a CMS object of type CompressedData, wrapped in a ContentInfo object and inserted into an application/pkcs7-mime entity with the smime-type compressed-data and the extension .p7z. Versions of S/MIME before 3.1 did not specify any use of CompressedData and will not recognize it.

The three formats can be nested, because each is a MIME entity that encapsulates other MIME entities. The operations can be applied in any order: signing first means the signatories are then securely obscured by the enveloping, while enveloping first means the signature is applied to the already encrypted content.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed message is usually sent as two parts, the readable text and its signature, so that a reader without S/MIME software can still see the text. An encrypted message holds one encrypted copy of the content key for each recipient.

sections.title: Choosing the Encryption and Handling Keys
sections.content:
Sending and receiving agents MUST support encryption and decryption with DES EDE3 CBC, called tripleDES. Receiving agents SHOULD support RC2 or a compatible algorithm at a key size of 40 bits, called RC2/40, and sending and receiving agents SHOULD support AES at key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits.

When a sending agent creates an encrypted message it has to decide which encryption to use, using the capabilities lists in messages received from the recipient and out-of-band information such as private agreements, user preferences and legal restrictions. The rules are ordered. Under rule 1, if the sending agent has received a set of capabilities for the recipient, it SHOULD use the first capability in the list, that is the one the recipient prefers most, that the sending agent knows how to encrypt. Under rule 2, if the sending agent knows neither the recipient's capabilities nor the recipient's version of S/MIME, it SHOULD use tripleDES, because it is a stronger algorithm and is required by version 3, and if it chooses not to, it SHOULD use RC2/40.

Before sending, the sending agent MUST decide whether it is willing to use weak encryption for the particular data in the message. If it is not, the agent MUST NOT use a weak algorithm such as RC2/40, and that decision overrides every other rule in the section. A sending agent controlled by a human SHOULD let the sender judge the risk of using RC2/40 and possibly choose a stronger method such as tripleDES. If the recipients of one message have capabilities that do not overlap, the sender is forced to send more than one message, and it should not send a copy of a message with weaker cryptography than it uses for the original, because someone watching the channel could then read the strong copy by decrypting the weak one.

All generated key pairs MUST be generated from a good source of non-deterministic random input, and the private key MUST be protected in a secure fashion. A user agent SHOULD generate RSA key pairs at a minimum key size of 768 bits and MUST NOT generate RSA key pairs less than 512 bits long. Keys longer than 1024 bits give better security but can stop some older receiving agents from verifying signatures, and a receiving agent SHOULD be able to verify signatures with keys of any size over 512 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender picks the encryption from the list of algorithms the recipient announced, and falls back to tripleDES when it knows nothing about the recipient. Weak 40-bit encryption may only be used if the sender is willing to accept the risk. Keys must be at least 512 bits, and 768 bits or more is recommended.

sections.title: Weak Encryption and Tampered Ciphertext
sections.content:
40-bit encryption is considered weak by most cryptographers, and using weak cryptography in S/MIME offers little actual security over sending plaintext. Using weak cryptography is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography, and when it is feasible, sending and receiving agents SHOULD tell each other the relative cryptographic strength of messages.

The RFC also warns about mixing strengths. If a sending agent sends the same message using different strengths of cryptography, an attacker watching the channel might be able to work out the contents of the strongly encrypted message by decrypting the weakly encrypted version. A sender SHOULD NOT send a copy of a message using weaker cryptography than the original.

Modification of the ciphertext can go undetected if authentication is not also used, which is the case when EnvelopedData is sent without being wrapped in SignedData, or when SignedData is enclosed inside it. The RFC points at RFC 3218 for more on the adaptive chosen ciphertext vulnerability in PKCS #1 Version 1.5 implementations.

Finally, the RFC notes that in some circumstances the use of the Diffie-Hellman key agreement scheme in a prime order subgroup of a large prime is vulnerable to small-subgroup attacks, and that methods exist to prevent them, described in RFC 2785.
sections.plainLanguage: Weak encryption is barely better than no encryption, and sending the same message twice with different strengths can leak the strong copy. Ciphertext can also be altered without anyone noticing unless the message is signed as well.

viz.caption: HOW TO TELL THAT A MESSAGE IS AN S/MIME MESSAGE

items.label: Any parameters, any file suffix
items.desc: The message carries a CMS object.

items.label: protocol="application/pkcs7-signature"
items.desc: The message carries a detached signature.

items.label: File suffix p7m, p7s, p7c or p7z
items.desc: The message was re-typed by a gateway, but the suffix shows it was S/MIME.

viz.caption: HOW A SENDER CHOOSES THE ENCRYPTION

items.title: Rule 1: known capabilities
items.text: Use the first algorithm in the recipient's list that the sender knows how to encrypt.

items.title: Rule 2: nothing known
items.text: Use tripleDES, or RC2/40 if tripleDES is not used.

items.title: Weak encryption
items.text: RC2/40 may only be used when the sender accepts the risk for that data.
